items.title: Ratio and equivalent ratios
items.content: Ratio \(a:b\) compares quantities in the same order and compatible units. Equivalent ratios multiply or divide both terms by the same nonzero number.

items.title: Proportion and variation
items.content: A proportion \(a:b=c:d\) means \(ad=bc\). Direct variation: \(y=kx\); inverse variation: \(y=k/x\), for nonzero values.

items.title: Dividing a quantity in a ratio
items.content: For \(a:b\), total parts are \(a+b\); shares are \(a/(a+b)\) and \(b/(a+b)\) of the total.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Label which quantity corresponds to each ratio term.
State assumptions such as constant speed, rate or productivity.

items.title: Simplify and interpret a ratio
items.content: Convert to the same units, then reduce. Worked example: 2 m : 50 cm = 200:50 = 4:1.

items.title: Divide a total in a ratio
items.content: Worked example: divide ₹840 in ratio 3:4. One part = 840/7 = ₹120; shares are ₹360 and ₹480.

items.title: Find a missing term in a proportion
items.content: Worked example: \(4:7=20:x\). Cross multiply: \(4x=140\), so \(x=35\).

items.title: Direct proportion
items.content: If each item has fixed cost, cost varies directly with quantity. Worked example: 5 kg cost ₹300; 8 kg cost \(300(8/5)=₹480\).

items.title: Inverse proportion
items.content: For fixed work, workers × time can be constant under equal productivity. Worked example: 6 workers take 10 days; 12 workers take \(6\cdot10/12=5\) days.

items.title: Scale and similar figures
items.content: A length scale factor \(k\) changes lengths by \(k\), areas by \(k^2\), and volumes by \(k^3\). Worked example: doubling every length multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8.

items.title: Simplify a ratio
items.content: Check units first. Worked example: 3 hours : 45 minutes = 180:45 = 4:1.

items.title: Divide in a given ratio
items.content: Add ratio parts, divide total by that number, then multiply each share. Worked example: divide 90 in ratio 2:3; one part is 18, so the shares are 36 and 54.

items.title: Direct or inverse word problem
items.content: Identify whether both quantities move together or oppositely; test with a simple change. Worked example: doubling equal workers for the same job halves the time, provided each worker has the same rate.

items.title: Scale factor problem
items.content: Apply the same multiplier to corresponding lengths. For area, square the length factor. Worked example: length scale 1:3 maps a 4 cm side to 12 cm; corresponding areas scale by 9.

items.title: Find a fourth proportional
items.content: Use cross multiplication and check the resulting ratio in the original order. Worked example: 2:5 = 8:x gives 2x = 40, hence x = 20.

items.title: Why equivalent ratios are equal
items.content: Multiplying both terms by \(k\) multiplies numerator and denominator of \(a/b\) by the same nonzero number, preserving the quotient.

items.title: Why cross multiplication works
items.content: From \(a/b=c/d\), multiply by \(bd\) (with nonzero denominators) to obtain \(ad=bc\).

items.title: Why inverse proportion has a constant product
items.content: If \(y=k/x\), then \(xy=k\). Doubling \(x\) halves \(y\), keeping the product fixed.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Comparing unlike units
items.content: Convert to one unit before simplifying a ratio.

items.title: Reversing order
items.content: A ratio a:b is not interchangeable with b:a.

items.title: Assuming inverse proportion
items.content: More workers reduce time only if work and productivity conditions stay fixed.

items.title: Scaling area linearly
items.content: Areas scale by the square of the length factor.

keyTakeaways: Ratios compare quantities in a fixed order.
Proportions can be solved by cross multiplication.
Direct variation keeps a quotient constant; inverse variation keeps a product constant.
A length scale factor is squared for area.
